name: Teop
confidence_why: The only modern description, Mosel and Thiesen's 2007 sketch grammar, states outright that stress and intonation have not been investigated, and the one older statement, Carter's 1952 grammatical notes reporting stress "usually on the penultimate syllable", is a brief mission-era note that no later source confirms, so any placement for Teop is a guess.

new_statements.rule_in_words: No rule given: the phonology chapter (by Mosel and Radtke) says explicitly that stress and intonation have not been investigated. The only stress information is incidental: two phonetic citations carry a final-syllable stress mark ([e.'na:] 'I', [ki'kis] 'strong'), and sec. 4.4 says the spelling of clitic groups 'largely depends on stress patterns', with examples marking stress on the article/plural clitics and on the first syllable of beiko 'child' (a-'maa 'beiko; 'te-a 'maa 'beiko). Nothing on position, weight, or contrast is stated.
new_statements.exceptions: None; the authors decline to state a rule. Sec. 4 header (p. 30): 'The analysis is based on the recordings LanguageLab_1 – LanguageLab_05, and Asu_01. For details see Radtke 2005 in this Documentation of the Teop Language.' a full-text search for stress/accent the full 148-pp text for stress/accent/prosod/intonation/tone finds nothing else (only a bare index keyword INTONATION). No lexical tone is mentioned; vowel length is contrastive.
new_statements.identity_note: Mosel & Thiesen 2007 describe the coastal dialect (project area between Tearuki and Kekesu; sec. 2.1.2, PDF p. 9; no dialect survey done). The unread MacKay 2021-22 SIL Orthography and Phonology Description is also labelled 'Coastal dialect' in its catalogue metadata. Carter 1952's title says 'the Teop dialect' in the older sense of Teop as a dialect/language, not a sub-dialect.
